title: Big O: time complexity, space complexity and growth rates
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Big O expresses an asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's resource use grows with input size. Common growth classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n squared) and O(2 to the n). Space complexity tracks additional storage under a stated convention.
understand.whyItMatters: Growth-rate analysis helps compare algorithm designs as input size increases, while measurements reveal real constants and hardware effects.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
Big O expresses an asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's resource use grows with input size. Common growth classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n squared) and O(2 to the n). Space complexity tracks additional storage under a stated convention.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The nested loops may compare a number of pairs proportional to n squared in the worst case, so the time complexity is O(n squared). The function uses O(1) additional space.

practise.guidedTask: Count comparisons for n equal to 4 and 10 in the no-duplicate case.
practise.independentTask: Compare the nested-loop duplicate check with a sorting-based or hash-based approach, stating assumptions and trade-offs.
hints: State whether the analysis is worst-case, average-case or best-case.
